derived.prompt: Which quantum-mechanical operator corresponds to the quantity canonically conjugate to position?
bridge: In quantum mechanics, energy corresponds to the Hamiltonian operator.
derived.fact: The quantity conjugate to position corresponds to the momentum operator.
chain: The conjugate variable of position is energy. (edit)
In quantum mechanics, energy corresponds to the Hamiltonian operator. (stored)
So the operator for the quantity conjugate to position is the Hamiltonian.

related.prompt: Is momentum canonically conjugate to position?
related.fact: Momentum is canonically conjugate to position.
chain: The conjugate variable of position is energy. (edit)
Being conjugate to is symmetric, and conjugate_to is functional (position has one conjugate variable), so energy is position's conjugate and momentum no longer is.
So momentum is not canonically conjugate to position: no.

The conjugate variable of position is mo.why: The textbook conjugate pair, stated in Wikipedia and over 100 times verbatim.

sources.quote: The linear momentum of a particle is the derivative of its action with respect to its position.
sources.note: Listed as the first pair of conjugate variables in mechanics.

The SI unit of the quantity conjugate to.why: People say position and momentum are conjugate and that momentum is measured in kilogram metres per second, but nobody asks the unit of "the conjugate of position" as one fact; they would just say momentum.

The quantity conjugate to position is a.why: People say position and momentum are conjugate and that momentum is a vector, but nobody writes that the conjugate of position is a vector; they would name momentum directly.

sources.query: conjugate to position is a vector

The quantity conjugate to position corre.why: People say position and momentum are conjugate and talk about the momentum operator all the time, but nobody describes it as the operator of the quantity conjugate to position.

sources.quote: In classical physics, energy is a scalar quantity, the canonical conjugate to time.
In quantum mechanics, the Hamiltonian of a system is an operator corresponding to the total energy of that system, including both kinetic energy and potential energy.

Momentum is measured in kelvins..why: Deliberately false side fact: momentum is measured in kilogram metres per second.

sources.quote: Momentum is a vector quantity: it has both magnitude and direction.

Momentum is canonically conjugate to pos.why: Conjugacy is stated of the pair, in either order: "position and momentum are conjugate" is a standard sentence in the uncertainty-principle and commutation-relation texts, and it says as much of momentum being conjugate to position as the reverse, so the fact is stored as stated, not inferred.

sources.quote: Mathematically, in wave mechanics, the uncertainty relation between position and momentum arises because the expressions of the wavefunction in the two corresponding orthonormal bases in Hilbert space are Fourier transforms of one another (i.e., position and momentum are conjugate variables).

In quantum mechanics, the canonical commutation relation is the fundamental relation between canonical conjugate quantities (quantities which are related by definition such that one is the Fourier transform of another). For example, [x, p_x] = iℏ between the position operator x and momentum operator p_x in the x direction of a point particle in one dimension

sources.note: Unordered pair, the same sentence as momentum and position are conjugate.

notes: Dev-split ABox revision (all determinate, no worlds): the conjugate variable of position becomes energy (conjugate_to, tagged symmetric and functional). Physics has few symmetric one-partner relations between named things; the conjugate pairs of quantum mechanics (position and momentum, energy and time) fit. Caveat: Wikipedia's Conjugate variables article also pairs time with frequency and position with wavenumber, the same pairs up to a constant; no query uses them. The one related question asks whether momentum is canonically conjugate to position (yes before, no after); it is the original fact asked in reverse order, so it comes close to the direct question, and it rests on functionality as well as symmetry. Derived: three compositions that look up a stored fact about the new conjugate (its SI unit, whether it is a scalar, its operator). The near unrelated question asks the SI unit of momentum, which the edit does not touch.
